added_lemmas.statement:
For every \(s\in[1,2]\), \(M\ge2\), \(0<\kappa_n\le1/8\), and
\(u\in[-1,1]\), the construction satisfies
\[
 \mathcal W_n^{\mathrm{fix}}\subset\mathcal P_n,
 \qquad c_{Q_u}=c_0,
 \qquad d_{Q_u}=\kappa_n,
 \qquad \theta_{Q_u}=u.
\]
Writing all divergences for the observed \(O_i\)-law, it also satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(Q_u^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})
 \le
 2\left(\frac{4H_s}{M}\right)^{1/s}
 n(\kappa_n|u|)^{2+1/s}
\]
and
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(Q_u^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})
 \le
 \left\{2\left(\frac{4H_s}{M}\right)^{1/s}
 n(\kappa_n|u|)^{2+1/s}\right\}^{1/2}.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Write \(a=(1-\kappa_n)/2\),
\(l=(1-\kappa_nu)/2\), and \(r=(1+\kappa_nu)/2\).
The type masses in \(\text{def:fixed-cutoff-bump-continuum}\) sum to one
and are nonnegative because \(0<\kappa_n\le1/8\).  Monotonicity follows
from \(D(0)=\mathbf 1\{R=A\}\) and
\(D(1)=\mathbf 1\{R\in\{A,C\}\}\).  Under assignment zero,
\[
 a r+\kappa_n\frac{1-u}{2}
 =\frac{1+\kappa_n}{2}l,
\]
whereas under assignment one,
\[
 a l+\kappa_n\frac{1+u}{2}
 =\frac{1+\kappa_n}{2}r.
\]
For assignment zero, the always-taker cell has outcome mean \(l\); the
first identity says that the combined never-taker--complier cell has the
same mean.  Thus \((D(0),Y(D(0)))\) has independent Bernoulli margins
\(((1-\kappa_n)/2,l)\).  The second identity gives independent margins
\(((1+\kappa_n)/2,r)\) for \((D(1),Y(D(1)))\).  Applying a common
type-independent binary kernel to the potential outcomes preserves this
independence for the actually assigned treatment.  Its denominators are
positive because every cutoff and target outcome mean is in
\([7/16,9/16]\).  This proves that the observable law is exactly the one
specified in the definition, without restricting the model class's
otherwise unrestricted treatment--outcome association.

The type masses do not depend on \(x\), so both potential-treatment
reduced forms are continuous at \(c_0\).  On either side, the Markov
kernel tends to the identity as \(x\to c_0\), since \(\psi(0)=1\).
Consequently, for each \(z\in\{0,1\}\), the reduced form
\(x\mapsto E_{Q_u}[Y(D(z))\mid X=x]\) tends from both sides to its value
under the common cutoff latent law.  This verifies the two causal
continuity assumptions.  The cutoff is interior, and the design is
uniform by construction.

It remains to check observable smoothness.  The function \(\psi\) is
continuously differentiable, its derivative is globally Lipschitz, and
direct differentiation on \([-1,1]\) gives
\(\|\psi\|_\infty\le1\), \(\|\psi'\|_\infty\le2\), and
\(\operatorname{Lip}(\psi')\le8\).  Hence \(H_s\le12\) for every
\(s\in[1,2]\).  If \(A=\kappa_n|u|/2\), direct rescaling gives
\[
 \left\|A\psi\!\left(\frac{\cdot-c_0}{h_u}\right)
 \right\|_{\mathcal H^s}
 \le A H_s(1+h_u^{-s})
 \le \frac34+\frac{M}{8}.
\]
Indeed, for \(s=1\) the Lipschitz seminorm is multiplied by
\(Ah_u^{-1}\); for \(s=1+\beta\), \(0<\beta\le1\), the derivative
supremum is multiplied by \(Ah_u^{-1}\) and its \(\beta\)-H\"older
seminorm by \(Ah_u^{-1-\beta}=Ah_u^{-s}\).  If \(h_u\le1\), both are
bounded by the displayed \(h_u^{-s}\) term, while if \(h_u>1\), both are
bounded by the displayed constant term.  Finally,
\(AH_sh_u^{-s}=M/8\) by the definition of \(h_u\), and
\(AH_s\le12/16=3/4\).
Adding the constant \(1/2\) gives a norm at most
\(5/4+M/8\le M\), using \(M\ge2\).  The treatment-side extensions are
constant and bounded by \(9/16\).  Thus all four one-sided extensions
belong to the declared radius-\(M\), order-\(s\) balls.  Their jumps at
\(c_0\) are \(\kappa_n\) and \(\kappa_nu\), respectively.  Therefore
the strength shell holds, and
\[
 d_{Q_u}=\kappa_n,
 \qquad y_{Q_u}=\kappa_nu,
 \qquad \theta_{Q_u}=y_{Q_u}/d_{Q_u}=u.
\]
The same value is obtained causally because the complier potential-
outcome means differ by \(u\).  This establishes membership in
\(\mathcal P_n\) and the asserted labels.

For the divergence calculation, \(Q_u\) and \(Q_0\) have the same
uniform \(X\)-law and the same conditional treatment law.  Conditional
independence in this witness therefore reduces their conditional joint
divergence to the outcome Bernoulli divergence.  If
\(p=1/2+v\), then
\[
 \operatorname{kl}(p,1/2)
 \le \chi^2(\operatorname{Ber}(p),\operatorname{Ber}(1/2))
 =4v^2.
\]
The inequality follows directly from \(\log z\le z-1\), applied to the
two likelihood-ratio values and averaged under \(\operatorname{Ber}(p)\).
The absolute outcome-mean displacement is
\(A\psi((x-c_0)/h_u)\).  Since \(0\le\psi\le1\), its support has the
displayed width, and \(\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z)^2\,dz\le2\), uniform
design yields
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(Q_u,Q_0)
 \le4A^2h_u\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z)^2\,dz
 \le2\kappa_n^2u^2h_u
 =2\left(\frac{4H_s}{M}\right)^{1/s}
   (\kappa_n|u|)^{2+1/s}.
\]
Independent sampling makes the log likelihood ratio a sum of \(n\)
one-observation log likelihood ratios; taking expectation gives exact
Kullback--Leibler tensorization and therefore the asserted
\(n\)-sample bound.

For completeness, the total-variation inequality used here follows
directly.  If \(p,q\) are densities, put
\(H^2(p,q)=\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\).  Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\(\operatorname{TV}(p,q)\le H(p,q)\).  The scalar inequality
\(-\log x\ge2(1-\sqrt x)\) gives
\(H^2(p,q)\le\operatorname{KL}(p,q)\).  Hellinger affinity
tensorizes, so
\[
 H^2(p^{\otimes n},q^{\otimes n})
 =2\left[1-\left(1-\frac{H^2(p,q)}2\right)^n\right]
 \le nH^2(p,q).
\]
Combining these three displayed inequalities with the one-observation
bound proves the asserted total-variation bound.

added_lemmas.statement:
Put \(a=1-\alpha\).  If \(\kappa_n\le1/16\), then
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge G_\alpha(\tau_n)
 =\begin{cases}
 2a-\dfrac{16}{3}\sqrt{\tau_n},
   &0\le\tau_n\le a^2/16,\\[6pt]
 \dfrac{a^3}{24\tau_n},&\tau_n>a^2/16.
 \end{cases}
\]
Moreover, there are constants \(c_{\mathrm{fix}}>0\) and
\(C_{\mathrm{low}}>0\), depending only on \(s\), \(M\), and
\(\alpha\), such that for every \(n\ge1\) and
\(0<\kappa_n\le1/8\),
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)
 \ge c_{\mathrm{fix}}\min\left\{1,\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n}\right\},
 \qquad
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge C_{\mathrm{low}}r_n.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix any interval rule \(I_n\) satisfying the honesty constraint in
\(\text{def:minimax-length}\), and first suppose \(\kappa_n\le1/16\).
By \(\text{prop:moving-cutoff-membership-kl}\), every \(P_t\) belongs to
\(\mathcal P_n\), has effect label \(t\), and satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P_t^{\otimes n},P_0^{\otimes n})
 \le4\sqrt{\tau_n|t|}.
\]
Honesty under \(P_t\) and the defining variational inequality for total
variation therefore imply, for every \(t\in[-1,1]\),
\[
 P_0^{\otimes n}\{t\in I_n\}
 \ge P_t^{\otimes n}\{t\in I_n\}
     -\operatorname{TV}(P_t^{\otimes n},P_0^{\otimes n})
 \ge1-\alpha-4\sqrt{\tau_n|t|}.
\]
The left side is nonnegative.  To justify the coverage integration
without any unrecorded interchange theorem, fix \(m\ge1\) and use the
equally spaced grid \(t_j=-1+2j/m\), \(j=0,\ldots,m\).  For every
connected \(I_n\subset[-1,1]\), the number of grid points in \(I_n\)
is at most \(1+m|I_n|/2\).  Hence, deterministically,
\[
 |I_n|\ge\frac2m\sum_{j=0}^m\mathbf 1\{t_j\in I_n\}-\frac2m.
\]
Taking expectations uses only linearity for this finite sum.  Applying
the preceding probability bound and then letting \(m\to\infty\), the
Riemann sums converge because
\(t\mapsto[1-\alpha-4\sqrt{\tau_n|t|}]_+\) is continuous.  Therefore
\[
 E_{P_0}|I_n|
 \ge2\int_0^1[1-\alpha-4\sqrt{\tau_nt}]_+\,dt
 =G_\alpha(\tau_n).
\]
Because \(P_0\in\mathcal P_n\), the worst-case expected length of every
honest rule is at least this quantity; taking the infimum over such rules
proves the first inequality.

To evaluate the integral, write \(a=1-\alpha\).  If
\(\tau_n\le a^2/16\), its integrand is positive throughout \([0,1]\),
and
\[
 2\int_0^1(a-4\sqrt{\tau_nt})\,dt
 =2a-\frac{16}{3}\sqrt{\tau_n}.
\]
If \(\tau_n>a^2/16\), the positive region ends at
\(t_0=a^2/(16\tau_n)\), and
\[
 2\int_0^{t_0}(a-4\sqrt{\tau_nt})\,dt
 =2\left(at_0-\frac83\sqrt{\tau_n}t_0^{3/2}\right)
 =\frac{a^3}{24\tau_n}.
\]
This proves the closed form in \(\text{def:integrated-slope-lower-function}\).

We next use the fixed-cutoff family.  Let
\[
 p_s=2+\frac1s,
 \qquad
 C_b=2\left(\frac{4H_s}{M}\right)^{1/s},
 \qquad
 \gamma=\min\left\{1,
 \left(\frac{(1-2\alpha)^2}{16C_b}\right)^{1/p_s}\right\},
\]
and choose the positive label
\[
 u_n=\gamma\min\left\{1,\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n}\right\}.
\]
Since \(\rho_n=n^{-s/(2s+1)}\), one has
\(n\rho_n^{p_s}=1\).  If \(\rho_n\le\kappa_n\), then
\(n(\kappa_nu_n)^{p_s}=\gamma^{p_s}\); if
\(\rho_n>\kappa_n\), the left side is at most
\(\gamma^{p_s}n\rho_n^{p_s}=\gamma^{p_s}\).  The preceding proposition
therefore gives
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(Q_{u_n}^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})
 \le\sqrt{C_b\gamma^{p_s}}
 \le\frac{1-2\alpha}{4}.
\]
Both laws are in \(\mathcal P_n\).  Honesty and total variation imply
under \(Q_0\)
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 Q_0^{\otimes n}\{0,u_n\in I_n\}
 &\ge1-Q_0^{\otimes n}\{0\notin I_n\}
       -Q_0^{\otimes n}\{u_n\notin I_n\}\\
 &\ge1-2\alpha-
 \operatorname{TV}(Q_{u_n}^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})
 \ge\frac34(1-2\alpha).
 \end{aligned}
\]
On this event, connectedness of \(I_n\subset[-1,1]\) forces
\(|I_n|\ge u_n\).  Consequently,
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P|I_n|
 \ge E_{Q_0}|I_n|
 \ge \frac34(1-2\alpha)\gamma
       \min\left\{1,\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n}\right\}.
\]
Taking the infimum proves the fixed-cutoff inequality with
\(c_{\mathrm{fix}}=3(1-2\alpha)\gamma/4>0\).

It remains to combine the two lower bounds.  The displayed formula for
\(G_\alpha\) implies, for every \(\tau>0\),
\[
 G_\alpha(\tau)
 \ge \frac{(1-\alpha)^3}{24}\min\{1,\tau^{-1}\}.
\]
Indeed, below the breakpoint its minimum is
\(2(1-\alpha)/3\), between the breakpoint and one the second branch is
at least \((1-\alpha)^3/24\), and above one the second branch equals
\((1-\alpha)^3/(24\tau)\).  Thus, when \(\kappa_n\le1/16\), the maximum
of the moving- and fixed-cutoff lower bounds is at least a positive
constant times
\[
 \min\left\{1,\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n}\right\}
 +\min\left\{1,\frac1{n\kappa_n^3}\right\}
 \ge
 \min\left\{1,\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n}
                 +\frac1{n\kappa_n^3}\right\}
 =r_n.
\]
When \(\kappa_n>1/16\), the location term is already absorbed by the
fixed-cutoff term, because
\[
 \frac{1}{n\kappa_n^3}
 \le256\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n},
\]
where \(n\rho_n=n^{(s+1)/(2s+1)}\ge1\) was used.  Hence
\(r_n\le257\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}\), and the fixed-cutoff inequality
again yields \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge C_{\mathrm{low}}r_n\) after reducing
the constant.  This proves the all-strength lower frontier.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
Using \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{prof}}\), construct \(I_n^{\mathrm{prof}}\)
and prove
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{P\in\mathcal P_n}
 P\{\theta_P\in I_n^{\mathrm{prof}}\}\ge1-\alpha
\]
for every strength sequence.  On each critical component of
\(\mathfrak R\) whose value is evaluated by \(\mathcal V_\alpha\), prove
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P|I_n^{\mathrm{prof}}|
 -L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Only on \(\mathfrak R_{\mathrm{cert}}\), prove
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P|I_n^{\mathrm{prof}}|
 \asymp L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\asymp r_n.
\]
The upper comparison must keep the local stochastic contribution
\(\rho_n/\kappa_n+1/(n\kappa_n^3)\) separate from the remainders
\(\zeta_n\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cont},n}\),
\(|\mathcal G_c|\exp[-C_{\mathrm{sep}}n\kappa_n^2h_n/4]\),
\(2\delta_n\), and twice the maximal probability of each fallback branch
in \(\text{def:worked-four-cell-grid}\); the last four expected-length
remainders must be \(o(r_n)\), and \(\zeta_n=o(1)\).  No upper rate or
critical constant is claimed from \(\mathsf{CR}(s,\kappa_\bullet)\), from
population separation, or from marginal profiling alone.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The recovered-regime lower-comparison request is no longer open: thm:integrated-and-bump-lower-frontier proves the stronger all-strength inequality under the unchanged model class. Removing that already-settled clause relocates the lower frontier to a proved theorem while preserving every unresolved honesty, upper-risk, fallback, and attainment obligation.

proposed.name: \mathcal W_n^{\mathrm{fix}}
proposed.construction:
Let
\[
 \psi(z)=(1-z^2)^2\mathbf 1\{|z|\le 1\},
 \qquad H_s=\|\psi\|_{\mathcal H^s(\mathbb R)},
\]
where the norm is the same standard H\"older norm used for the radius-
\(M\) balls in \(\text{ass:observable-holder-extensions}\).  Put
\(h_0=0\); for \(u\ne0\), put
\[
 h_u=\left(\frac{4H_s\kappa_n|u|}{M}\right)^{1/s}.
\]
Under \(Q_u\), the observations are independent and identically
distributed, \(X\) is uniform on \([0,1]\), and the cutoff is
\(c_0=1/2\).  Conditional on \(X=x\), the observed variables \(D\) and
\(Y\) are independent Bernoulli variables.
The treatment mean is \((1-\kappa_n)/2\) for \(x<c_0\) and
\((1+\kappa_n)/2\) for \(x\ge c_0\).  For \(u\ne0\), the outcome mean is
\[
 \frac12-\frac{\kappa_nu}{2}
 \psi\!\left(\frac{x-c_0}{h_u}\right)\quad(x<c_0),
 \qquad
 \frac12+\frac{\kappa_nu}{2}
 \psi\!\left(\frac{x-c_0}{h_u}\right)\quad(x\ge c_0).
\]
For \(u=0\), the outcome mean is \(1/2\) on both sides.

The full-data lift is defined as follows.  At the cutoff, assign type
masses \((1-\kappa_n)/2,\kappa_n,(1-\kappa_n)/2\) to \(A,C,N\),
respectively.  Always-takers have a common binary potential outcome of
mean \((1-\kappa_nu)/2\), never-takers have a common binary potential
outcome of mean \((1+\kappa_nu)/2\), and complier potential outcomes have
means \((1-u)/2\) and \((1+u)/2\) under treatment zero and one,
respectively.  Away from the cutoff, start from this common cutoff law.
On the observed side \(z\), apply to both binary potential outcomes the
same type-independent binary Markov kernel that maps their relevant
cutoff-side outcome mean \(b\) to the displayed target mean \(g\): when
\(g\ge b\), retain every one and change a zero to one with probability
\((g-b)/(1-b)\); when \(g<b\), retain every zero and retain a one with
probability \(g/b\).  Use conditionally independent auxiliary coins.
Let
\[
 \mathcal W_n^{\mathrm{fix}}=\{Q_u:u\in[-1,1]\}.
\]

proposed_core_edits.reason: This explicit causal lift and observable bump family is the same-class witness requested for the fixed-cutoff minimax lower term.
The retained label-dependent coverage integral has the directive's explicit piecewise closed form.

proposed_core_edits.proposed: \(I_n^{\mathrm{prof}}=\operatorname{hull}\{\vartheta\in\Theta:\inf_{c\in\mathcal G_c}\Delta_n(c,\vartheta)\le\Gamma_n(\delta_n)\}\). The proved minimax converse is \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\gtrsim r_n\) over the full declared strength shell; the matching profile upper comparison \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\asymp r_n\) remains proposed only on \(\mathfrak R_{\mathrm{cert}}\).

open_obligations.what_is_open: After relocating the proved all-strength lower comparison, uniform continuum honesty and minimax expected-length attainment for \(I_n^{\mathrm{prof}}\), including the separately displayed upper-rate remainders and fallback probabilities, remain open.
open_obligations.obstruction: Exact-grid method-of-types calibration and population profile separation do not transfer a continuously indexed true cutoff and effect to the candidate-specific grids and inner--outer sieves. The frozen core still lacks uniform control of the moved-discontinuity strip, localized stochastic profile width, certificate and solver fallbacks, and the critical-face decision value; the unresolved critical experiment also prevents equality with \(L_n^\star\) on finite-positive faces.
open_obligations.attempted: The exact-grid feasible-truth event was combined with the established deterministic false-split gap, and the lower-risk part was attacked separately by the moving-cutoff coverage integral and the new fixed-cutoff bump continuum. This closes the entire minimax lower frontier but supplies no uniform continuum-transfer or profile upper-risk theorem.
open_obligations.partial_result:
The all-strength minimax lower comparison is now closed separately:
\(\text{thm:integrated-and-bump-lower-frontier}\) proves
\(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge C_{\mathrm{low}}r_n\) for the entire declared
strength shell.  Its moving-cutoff component gives the stronger explicit
bound \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge G_\alpha(\tau_n)\), and its fixed-cutoff
bump component gives
\(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge c_{\mathrm{fix}}
\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}\).  Independently, the established exact-grid
calibration proposition accepts a grid-aligned true pair with conditional
probability at least
\(1-\delta_n/(|\mathcal G_c||\mathcal G_\vartheta|)\), and returning
\(\Theta\) on every listed fallback preserves that coverage.  The
established population separation theorem supplies the deterministic gap
\(C_{\mathrm{sep}}\kappa_n^2\min\{|c-c_P|,h_n\}\).  These are the complete
lower, exact-grid calibration, and population-localization layers; they
do not prove continuum honesty or the profile interval's upper risk.

prose_updates.tldr: For fuzzy regression discontinuity with a weak compliance jump and unknown cutoff, cutoff recovery and causal-effect informativeness are distinct. The moving-cutoff continuum now gives the explicit finite-sample lower value \(G_\alpha(\tau_n)\), and a causal-valid fixed-cutoff bump continuum gives the nonparametric term \(\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}\). Together they prove the all-strength converse \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\gtrsim r_n\) under the unchanged binary H\"older-margin class, while the existing upper bound gives the exact flat-face limit \(2(1-\alpha)\). Finite-grid four-cell calibration remains valid for every compatible treatment--outcome association, including singular cells. The open kernel is the \(s=1\) critical decision value and a continuum-honest, support-wide profile interval with controlled stochastic, discretization, certificate, and fallback remainders; no profile upper rate or finite-positive critical value is claimed as proved.

project_justification.gap: Known-cutoff weak-fuzzy inference, sharp-RD unknown-cutoff rates, generic weak-identification decision theory, and Bayesian propagation of cutoff uncertainty have been developed separately. None supplies an all-strength minimax converse together with an attaining honest connected interval when the cutoff and fuzzy denominator weaken jointly; the converse is now proved here, whereas attainment remains open.
project_justification.niche: The preserved binary uniform-design class makes two complementary causal lifts explicit while leaving the observable treatment--outcome association unrestricted. A moving-cutoff continuum measures slope-location ambiguity and a fixed-cutoff compact bump measures ordinary nonparametric jump difficulty, producing a nonregular location/effect problem that is neither a fixed-boundary modulus problem nor a parametric unknown-break problem.
project_justification.fill: The project proves the lower frontier by combining the integrated moving-cutoff value \(G_\alpha(\tau_n)\) with a same-class fixed-cutoff bump bound, yielding \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\gtrsim r_n\) for every declared strength. It also defines a support-wide four-cell profile and coarsened exact calibration that leave association free. The matching upper frontier, the complete critical experiment, and a total attaining interval remain the stated unresolved contribution.

prose_updates.related_work: Hahn, Todd, and van der Klaauw (2001) supply the local Wald identification argument. Feir, Lemieux, and Marmer (2016) and Noack and Rothe (2024, Theorem 1) give weak-identification-robust inference at a fixed known cutoff; they do not address translated cutoff/effect ambiguity. The new fixed-cutoff bump continuum recovers the usual nonparametric weak-denominator difficulty inside the present binary class, while the moving-cutoff continuum adds the distinct \(1/(n\kappa_n^3)\) difficulty and its explicit integrated value \(G_\alpha\). Porter and Yu (2015, Sections 3--5) and Tuvaandorj (2020, Sections 3--4) study unknown-location behavior predominantly in sharp designs, without this weak causal ratio or connected honest-length criterion. Elliott and M\"uller (2014, Sections 2.1--2.3) motivate process experiments for moderate unknown breaks, but do not solve the present H\"older-margin decision problem. Andrews and Mikusheva (2016, Theorem 1) and Andrews and Mikusheva (2022, Theorem 1 and Section 4) inform nuisance calibration and weak-decision analysis; Armstrong and Koles{\'a}r (2018, Theorem 3.1 and Appendix A.4) connect testing power to expected length over convex fixed-index classes. None of these results proves the still-open support-wide profile upper bound over the translated nonconvex union. Arai, Hsu, Kitagawa, Mourifi{\'e}, and Wan (2022, Section 2) motivate retaining the full joint outcome--treatment law. Kowalska, van de Wiel, and van der Pas (2025 version, Sections 3 and 6) propagate unknown-cutoff uncertainty in a Bayesian model without uniform frequentist honesty or minimax length.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The model has no outcome-variance, null-residual-variance, covariance-eigenvalue, or joint-cell positivity floor, and the new lower bound adds none. The proved results now include the moving-cutoff causal lift and its Kullback--Leibler bound, the explicit integrated lower value \(G_\alpha(\tau_n)\), the exact flat-face limit, the fixed-cutoff compact-bump causal lift and its \(n(\kappa_n|u|)^{2+1/s}\) divergence bound, and the all-strength minimax converse \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\gtrsim r_n\). Exact finite-grid four-cell calibration and population false-split separation are also proved, uniformly over permitted binary treatment--outcome associations. These facts do not establish continuum honesty, an upper expected-length rate, or attainment by \(I_n^{\mathrm{prof}}\). The finite-positive decision values, full-model least favorability, continuum discretization, localized stochastic profile bound, and negligible fallback risk remain open. A matching upper comparison is still only a proposed goal on \(\mathfrak R_{\mathrm{cert}}\). No smoothness of joint cells, conditional independence for the full class, association separation, cross-side derivative matching, oracle cutoff, or known association nuisance is imposed.

statement_notes.justification: The two legal causal continua isolate the location-slope and fixed-cutoff nonparametric sources of difficulty and combine to prove the complete lower half of the candidate all-strength frontier.
statement_notes.gap: Known-cutoff weak-fuzzy procedures do not supply the moving-location term, while sharp unknown-cutoff rates do not supply the weak causal-ratio term; the theorem derives both within one unchanged full model.
statement_notes.consumer: An analyst obtains a design-independent impossibility benchmark: no honest connected interval can beat \(r_n\), even before the proposed profile procedure is shown to attain it.

statement_notes.justification: With the minimax lower frontier settled separately, the remaining task is a single total interval that converts finite-grid calibration into continuum-uniform honesty and a matching upper expected-length guarantee.
statement_notes.gap: Andrews and Mikusheva (2016) condition out a functional nuisance in Gaussian-process moment models, while Feir, Lemieux, and Marmer (2016) and Noack and Rothe (2024) invert weak-identification-robust tests at a known cutoff. None supplies the required certified four-cell continuum transfer, fallback control, or critical-face attainment under an unknown cutoff.
statement_notes.consumer: The interval would give a frequentist benchmark for unknown or administratively uncertain eligibility thresholds, including the binary HIV-retention application studied by Kowalska, van de Wiel, and van der Pas.

proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(a=1-\alpha\).  We first exhibit an admissible rule for the upper bound.  Define
\[
 I_n^0(O_1,\ldots,O_n)=
 \begin{cases}
 \Theta,&X_1>\alpha,\\
 \varnothing,&X_1\le\alpha.
 \end{cases}
\]
The empty set and \(\Theta\) are connected subsets of \(\Theta\), and the rule is measurable.  By \(\texttt{ass:uniform-running-variable}\), for every \(P\in\mathcal P_n\),
\[
 P\{\theta_P\in I_n^0\}=P(X_1>\alpha)=1-\alpha,
 \qquad
 E_P|I_n^0|=2(1-\alpha).
\]
Thus \(I_n^0\) is feasible in \(\texttt{def:minimax-length}\), and
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\le 2(1-\alpha).
\]

For the converse, let \(I_n\) be any rule feasible in \(\texttt{def:minimax-length}\).  By \(\texttt{prop:moving-cutoff-membership-kl}\), for every \(t\in[-1,1]\), the law \(P_t\) belongs to \(\mathcal P_n\), its estimand is \(\theta_{P_t}=t\), and
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P_t^{\otimes n},P_0^{\otimes n})
 \le 4\sqrt{\tau_n|t|}.
\]
Honesty and the defining event bound for total variation therefore imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 P_0^{\otimes n}\{t\in I_n\}
 &\ge P_t^{\otimes n}\{t\in I_n\}
      -\operatorname{TV}(P_t^{\otimes n},P_0^{\otimes n})\\
 &\ge a-4\sqrt{\tau_n|t|}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The left side is nonnegative, so it is at least \([a-4\sqrt{\tau_n|t|}]_+\).  For every realization of the interval, its Lebesgue length is the integral of its membership indicator.  Integrating this nonnegative identity with respect to the joint law of the sample and Lebesgue measure gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 E_{P_0^{\otimes n}}|I_n|
 &=\int_{-1}^1P_0^{\otimes n}\{t\in I_n\}\,dt\\
 &\ge 2\int_0^1[a-4\sqrt{\tau_n t}]_+\,dt\\
 &\ge 2[a-4\sqrt{\tau_n}]_+.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Because \(P_0\in\mathcal P_n\), taking first the supremum over \(P\in\mathcal P_n\) and then the infimum over all honest rules proves
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge2[1-\alpha-4\sqrt{\tau_n}]_+.
\]

If \(\tau_n\to0\), the preceding lower bound and the displayed upper bound both converge to \(2(1-\alpha)\), proving the first limit.  Finally, fix \(s>1\) and suppose that \(\lambda_n\) remains in a compact subset of \((0,\infty)\).  In particular, \(\lambda_n\) is bounded above.  If \(\kappa_n\not\to0\), then along some subsequence \(\kappa_n\ge\epsilon>0\), whence
\[
 \lambda_n
 =\frac{n\kappa_n^{2+1/s}}{\log(e/\kappa_n)}
 \longrightarrow\infty,
\]
contradicting boundedness.  Hence \(\kappa_n\to0\).  The defining identity for \(\lambda_n\) gives
\[
 \tau_n
 =\lambda_n\kappa_n^{1-1/s}\log(e/\kappa_n).
\]
Since \(1-1/s>0\), the elementary power--log limit implies \(\kappa_n^{1-1/s}\log(e/\kappa_n)\to0\).  Boundedness of \(\lambda_n\) therefore yields \(\tau_n\to0\).  Moreover, \(\kappa_n\to0\) ensures \(\kappa_n\le1/16\) eventually, so the first limit applies to the tail of the sequence.

added_lemmas.statement:
There are constants \(u_0=u_0(s,M)\in(0,1]\) and \(C_b=C_b(s,M)<\infty\), and an i.i.d. continuum \(\{Q_u:|u|\le u_0\}\subset\mathcal P_n\), with the following properties.  Every member has cutoff \(c_{Q_u}=c_0\), compliance jump \(d_{Q_u}=\kappa_n\), and causal label \(\theta_{Q_u}=u\).  Conditionally on \(X=x\), its observed \(D\) and \(Y\) are independent Bernoulli variables.  The treatment mean is \((1-\kappa_n)/2\) to the left of \(c_0\) and \((1+\kappa_n)/2\) to the right.  With \(\phi(v)=(1-v^2)_+^2\), \(A_u=\kappa_n|u|\), and a width \(h_u\) proportional to \((A_u/M)^{1/s}\), the outcome means for \(u\ne0\) are
\[
 m_u^-(x)=\frac12-\frac{\kappa_nu}{2}\phi\!\left(\frac{x-c_0}{h_u}\right),
 \qquad
 m_u^+(x)=\frac12+\frac{\kappa_nu}{2}\phi\!\left(\frac{x-c_0}{h_u}\right),
\]
on the left and right sides, respectively; for \(u=0\), both means equal \(1/2\).  Moreover,
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(Q_u^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})
 \le C_b n(\kappa_n|u|)^{2+1/s},
 \qquad
 \chi^2(Q_u^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})
 \le \exp\!\{C_b n(\kappa_n|u|)^{2+1/s}\}-1.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Write \(\phi(v)=(1-v^2)_+^2\).  On \((-1,1)\),
\[
 \phi'(v)=-4v(1-v^2),\qquad \phi''(v)=-4+12v^2,
\]
whereas \(\phi\) and \(\phi'\) vanish continuously at \(-1\) and \(1\).  Thus \(\phi\) is Lipschitz, \(\phi'\) is globally Lipschitz, and, for every fixed \(s\in[1,2]\), direct rescaling supplies a finite constant \(B_s\ge1\) such that, for \(0<h\le1\) and every scalar \(a\),
\[
 \left\|a\phi\!\left(\frac{\cdot-c_0}{h}\right)\right\|_{\mathcal H^s}
 \le B_s|a|h^{-s}.
\]
For \(s=1\) this follows from the bound on \(\phi'\).  For \(1<s\le2\), writing \(\beta=s-1\), the Lipschitz and boundedness bounds on \(\phi'\) imply \([\phi']_\beta<\infty\), and the displayed scaling follows by the chain rule.  This verifies the required assertion without an external smoothness result.

Set
\[
 u_0=\min\!\left\{1,\frac{4M}{B_s4^s}\right\},
 \qquad
 h_u=\left(\frac{2B_sA_u}{M}\right)^{1/s}
 \quad (u\ne0).
\]
Because \(\kappa_n\le1/8\) and \(|u|\le u_0\),
\[
 h_u^s=\frac{2B_s\kappa_n|u|}{M}
 \le \frac{B_su_0}{4M}
 \le4^{-s},
\]
so \(h_u\le1/4\).  Hence the two observed half-bumps are supported inside \([0,1]\).  Their \(\mathcal H^s\) seminorm contribution is at most
\[
 B_s\frac{A_u}{2}h_u^{-s}=\frac M4.
\]
The constant baseline contributes at most \(1/2\), and \(M\ge2\); consequently each outcome branch has a radius-\(M\) H\"older extension.  The treatment branches are constant and bounded by one, so they also have radius at most \(M\).  All displayed Bernoulli means lie in \([0,1]\), because \(A_u\le1/8\).

We next construct the full-data causal lift.  At \(X=c_0\), assign response-type probabilities
\[
 Q_u(R=A)=Q_u(R=N)=\frac{1-\kappa_n}{2},
 \qquad Q_u(R=C)=\kappa_n,
\]
and define \(D(z)\) from the monotone response type.  For always-takers and never-takers, take a common binary potential outcome under both treatment states, with respective means
\[
 \frac{1-\kappa_nu}{2}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \frac{1+\kappa_nu}{2}.
\]
For compliers, choose binary potential outcomes with means
\[
 E_{Q_u}[Y(0)\mid R=C,X=c_0]=\frac{1-u}{2},
 \qquad
 E_{Q_u}[Y(1)\mid R=C,X=c_0]=\frac{1+u}{2}.
\]
A joint binary pair with these two marginals exists, for example by conditional independence.  Under assignment \(z=0\), the treated units are precisely the always-takers.  Their outcome mean is \((1-\kappa_nu)/2\), and the mean among the untreated never-taker--complier mixture is
\[
 \frac{(1-\kappa_n)(1+\kappa_nu)+2\kappa_n(1-u)}{2(1+\kappa_n)}
 =\frac{1-\kappa_nu}{2}.
\]
Thus \(D(0)\) and \(Y(D(0))\) are independent, and the marginal outcome mean is \((1-\kappa_nu)/2\).  Under assignment \(z=1\), the untreated units are precisely the never-takers, and the analogous treated-mixture calculation is
\[
 \frac{(1-\kappa_n)(1-\kappa_nu)+2\kappa_n(1+u)}{2(1+\kappa_n)}
 =\frac{1+\kappa_nu}{2}.
\]
Hence \(D(1)\) and \(Y(D(1))\) are independent, with marginal outcome mean \((1+\kappa_nu)/2\).

For \(x\ne c_0\), apply to every potential-outcome bit the same type-independent refresh kernel: retain the cutoff bit with probability \(\phi((x-c_0)/h_u)\) and otherwise replace it by an independent fair bit.  On the assigned left side this maps \((1-\kappa_nu)/2\) to \(m_u^-(x)\); on the assigned right side it maps \((1+\kappa_nu)/2\) to \(m_u^+(x)\).  Because the kernel is common across response types, the observed conditional independence of \(D\) and \(Y\) is retained.  Because its retention probability tends to one as \(x\to c_0\), both \(x\mapsto E_{Q_u}[D(z)\mid X=x]\) and \(x\mapsto E_{Q_u}[Y(D(z))\mid X=x]\) are continuous at \(c_0\), for each \(z\).  Take \(X\) uniform on \([0,1]\), set \(Z=\mathbf 1\{X\ge c_0\}\), impose consistency and exclusion, and take independent copies across units.  The cutoff is interior, monotonicity holds by construction, and
\[
 d_{Q_u}=\frac{1+\kappa_n}{2}-\frac{1-\kappa_n}{2}=\kappa_n,
 \qquad
 y_{Q_u}=m_u^+(c_0)-m_u^-(c_0)=\kappa_nu.
\]
Thus the strength shell holds and \(\theta_{Q_u}=y_{Q_u}/d_{Q_u}=u\).  The conditional complier contrast is also directly
\[
 E_{Q_u}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid R=C,X=c_0]=u.
\]
All member properties in \(\texttt{def:model-class}\) have now been checked, so \(Q_u\in\mathcal P_n\).

It remains to establish the divergences.  Under \(Q_0\), the conditional outcome probability is \(1/2\).  Under \(Q_u\), write it as \(1/2+\delta_u(x)\), where \(|\delta_u(x)|\le A_u/2\).  For \(|\delta|<1/2\), the scalar inequality \(\log(1+v)\le v\) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{kl}\!\left(\frac12+\delta,\frac12\right)
 &=\left(\frac12+\delta\right)\log(1+2\delta)
   +\left(\frac12-\delta\right)\log(1-2\delta)\\
 &\le4\delta^2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The treatment factors cancel in the likelihood ratio, and uniformity of \(X\), compact support of \(\phi\), and \(0\le\phi\le1\) yield
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(Q_u,Q_0)
 \le A_u^2\int_0^1\phi^2\!\left(\frac{x-c_0}{h_u}\right)dx
 \le2A_u^2h_u.
\]
Additivity under independent sampling therefore gives
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(Q_u^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})
 \le 2\left(\frac{2B_s}{M}\right)^{1/s}nA_u^{2+1/s}.
\]
For the chi-square bound, the one-observation likelihood ratio for the outcome factor is \(1+2(2Y-1)\delta_u(X)\).  Consequently
\[
 \chi^2(Q_u,Q_0)=4\int_0^1\delta_u(x)^2dx\le2A_u^2h_u.
\]
Factorization of the squared likelihood ratio under the product law gives
\[
 \chi^2(Q_u^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})
 =\{1+\chi^2(Q_u,Q_0)\}^n-1
 \le\exp\!\left\{2\left(\frac{2B_s}{M}\right)^{1/s}nA_u^{2+1/s}\right\}-1.
\]
Taking \(C_b=2(2B_s/M)^{1/s}\) proves both claims.  The case \(u=0\) follows by defining \(Q_0\) with outcome mean identically \(1/2\), in which case both divergences vanish.

added_lemmas.statement:
There is a constant \(C_{\mathrm{low}}=C_{\mathrm{low}}(s,M,\alpha)>0\) such that, for every \(n\) and every \(0<\kappa_n\le1/8\),
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge C_{\mathrm{low}}r_n.
\]
In addition, whenever \(\kappa_n\le1/16\), writing \(a=1-\alpha\),
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)
 \ge 2\int_0^1[a-4\sqrt{\tau_n t}]_+\,dt
 =
 \begin{cases}
 2a-\dfrac{16}{3}\sqrt{\tau_n},&0\le\tau_n\le a^2/16,\\[5pt]
 \dfrac{a^3}{24\tau_n},&\tau_n>a^2/16.
 \end{cases}
\]
Thus the moving-cutoff contribution is bounded below by a positive constant times \(\min\{1,1/(n\kappa_n^3)\}\), while the fixed-cutoff contribution is bounded below by a positive constant times \(\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Let \(I_n\) be any confidence-interval rule feasible in \(\texttt{def:minimax-length}\), and set \(a=1-\alpha\).  If \(\kappa_n\le1/16\), \(\texttt{prop:moving-cutoff-membership-kl}\) gives, for every \(t\in[-1,1]\),
\[
 P_0^{\otimes n}\{t\in I_n\}
 \ge P_t^{\otimes n}\{t\in I_n\}
       -\operatorname{TV}(P_t^{\otimes n},P_0^{\otimes n})
 \ge a-4\sqrt{\tau_n|t|}.
\]
After taking the positive part and integrating the interval-membership identity over \([-1,1]\),
\[
 E_{P_0^{\otimes n}}|I_n|
 \ge2\int_0^1[a-4\sqrt{\tau_n t}]_+\,dt.
\]
If \(\tau_n\le a^2/16\), the integrand is nonnegative on all of \([0,1]\), so
\[
 2\int_0^1(a-4\sqrt{\tau_n t})dt
 =2a-\frac{16}{3}\sqrt{\tau_n}.
\]
If \(\tau_n>a^2/16\), it is positive exactly for \(0\le t<a^2/(16\tau_n)\), and hence
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 2\int_0^{a^2/(16\tau_n)}(a-4\sqrt{\tau_n t})dt
 &=2\left\{\frac{a^3}{16\tau_n}-
 \frac{a^3}{24\tau_n}\right\}\\
 &=\frac{a^3}{24\tau_n}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Since \(P_0\in\mathcal P_n\), minimization over honest \(I_n\) proves the displayed moving-cutoff lower bound.  Its piecewise formula also shows, for every \(\tau_n\ge0\),
\[
 2\int_0^1[a-4\sqrt{\tau_n t}]_+dt
 \ge \frac{a^3}{24}\min\{1,\tau_n^{-1}\},
\]
with the convention \(\tau_n^{-1}=+\infty\) at zero: below the breakpoint the left side is at least \(2a/3\), and above it the formula is \(a^3/(24\tau_n)\).

We next use \(\texttt{prop:fixed-cutoff-bump-continuum}\).  Put \(p=2+1/s\), and choose a constant
\[
 \gamma=\min\!\left\{u_0,
 \left[\frac{\log\{1+(1-2\alpha)^2\}}{C_b}\right]^{1/p}\right\}>0.
\]
Define
\[
 u_n=\gamma\min\left\{1,\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n}\right\}.
\]
Then \(0<u_n\le u_0\), and, because \(n\rho_n^{2+1/s}=1\),
\[
 n(\kappa_nu_n)^p
 =\gamma^p n\min\{\kappa_n,\rho_n\}^p
 \le\gamma^p.
\]
Let \(L=dQ_{u_n}^{\otimes n}/dQ_0^{\otimes n}\).  The definition of total variation and Cauchy--Schwarz give directly
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(Q_{u_n}^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})
 =\frac12E_{Q_0^{\otimes n}}|L-1|
 \le\frac12\{E_{Q_0^{\otimes n}}(L-1)^2\}^{1/2}
 \le\frac{1-2\alpha}{2},
\]
where the last inequality follows from the chi-square bound and the definition of \(\gamma\).  Honesty under \(Q_0\) and \(Q_{u_n}\), followed by the total-variation event bound, gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 Q_0^{\otimes n}\{0\in I_n\}&\ge1-\alpha,\\
 Q_0^{\otimes n}\{u_n\in I_n\}&\ge1-\alpha-
 \operatorname{TV}(Q_{u_n}^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n}).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the union bound yields
\[
 Q_0^{\otimes n}\{0,u_n\in I_n\}
 \ge1-2\alpha-operatorname{TV}(Q_{u_n}^{\otimes n},Q_0^{\otimes n})
 \ge\frac{1-2\alpha}{2}.
\]
Connectedness implies \(|I_n|\ge u_n\) on this event.  Since \(Q_0\in\mathcal P_n\), taking expectations, the supremum over the model, and the infimum over honest rules gives
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)
 \ge c_f\min\left\{1,\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n}\right\},
 \qquad
 c_f=\frac{\gamma(1-2\alpha)}2>0.
\]

It remains to combine the two contributions.  Write
\[
 A_n=\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n},\qquad
 B_n=\frac1{n\kappa_n^3}=\tau_n^{-1}.
\]
When \(\kappa_n\le1/16\), the two bounds just proved imply
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)
 \ge \min\left\{c_f,\frac{a^3}{24}\right\}
 \max\{\min(1,A_n),\min(1,B_n)\}.
\]
Since
\[
 \min(1,A_n+B_n)
 \le\min(1,A_n)+\min(1,B_n)
 \le2\max\{\min(1,A_n),\min(1,B_n)\},
\]
this is at least a positive constant times
\(r_n=\min\{1,A_n+B_n\}\).

Finally suppose \(1/16<\kappa_n\le1/8\).  The purported location term is then absorbed by the fixed-cutoff term, because
\[
 \frac{B_n}{A_n}
 =\frac1{n\kappa_n^2\rho_n}
 \le256\,n^{-(s+1)/(2s+1)}
 \le256.
\]
Consequently
\[
 r_n=\min(1,A_n+B_n)
 \le257\min(1,A_n),
\]
and the fixed-cutoff lower bound gives \(L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge(c_f/257)r_n\).  Taking \(C_{\mathrm{low}}\) to be the minimum of the positive constants obtained in the two cases completes the proof.
